cues.text: Morning, Sergeant. I need one exhibit logged out to room 3B.
That's a court seal. Nobody brought anything like that in here.
I sealed it downstairs this morning, after the inventory was finished.
Downstairs is my property room. Who let you in down there?
The same court order you signed for six weeks ago, Sergeant.
I signed for an inventory. Counting boxes. Not carrying things out.
Nothing's leaving the building. It goes upstairs to 3B by eleven.
Then it goes in my ledger first, with what's inside it.
The ledger asks for an exhibit number. Not for contents.
In this room, the ledger asks what I tell it to.
Deputy, is your camera running? I'd like it to keep running.
It runs the whole shift, ma'am. I don't switch it off.
Nobody asked you, Moreno. Stand where you're standing and stay quiet.
Exhibit number is on the tape. Forty-one dash seventeen dash A.
I can read tape. I'm asking what that seal is protecting.
It's protecting the contents from everyone who isn't the grand jury.
Grand jury. In my building, and nobody thought to tell me.
Nobody is supposed to tell you. That's what sealed means, Sergeant.
Then it sits right here until somebody tells me something true.
It's ten forty now. I'm expected upstairs in twenty minutes, Sergeant.
Then you'd better start talking. Twenty minutes is all you've got.
I'll talk. But nothing I say will be about what's inside.
Start with your name. Everybody who signs this ledger gives one.
My name is on the court order in your file drawer.
I'm not opening drawers. I'm asking you, standing at my counter.
Naomi Bell. Evidence auditor, under contract to the federal court.
Federal. So somebody downtown sent you here to count my boxes.
A judge sent me. I've counted every box, and every shelf.
Six weeks in my basement, and I never heard your name.
That was deliberate. People behave normally when nobody knows who's watching.
You hear that, Moreno? She's been watching us. Write that down.
Write down what, Sarge? She hasn't done anything I can write.
You write what I tell you. That's what a report is.
If you doubt me, call the grand jury clerk. Extension four-one-one.
I don't call upstairs because a stranger hands me a number.
Then call the switchboard and ask for 3B. Same answer, Sergeant.
I've worked this building fourteen years. I know who belongs here.
You know who used to belong. Things changed six weeks ago.
What changed six weeks ago? Go on, say it plainly.
A judge ordered an audit. That's plain. That's all I'll say.
Put some identification on the counter. Then we'll see what's plain.
You'll get my ID. You won't get what's under the seal.
Moreno, if she walks out with that, you stop her. Understood?
Stop her how, Sarge? She hasn't broken any rule I know.
She's breaking mine. In this room, that's the one that counts.
Bell. Washington address. You drove four hours to count boxes?
I drove four hours every Monday. I left every Friday afternoon.
And slept where? Not anywhere in this county, or I'd know.
The motel by the interstate. Room twelve. Check that too.
Sit down over there. This takes as long as it takes.
It takes about a minute. I'll stand, if that's all right.
It isn't all right. Chairs are right there. Use one.
Ma'am, would you like some water? There's a cooler outside.
No, thank you. I'd rather nobody leaves the room right now.
Understood. Then I'll stay right here by the door, ma'am.
Funny. A woman alone, sealed packet, worried about who leaves rooms.
Not funny. Careful. You'd want the same if it were yours.
No warrants. No tickets. Not one parking violation. Nothing at all.
That's usually what it says about people who mind their business.
Or people who know how to keep their names off screens.
You'd know more about keeping names off records than I would.
What's that supposed to mean? Say it again for the camera.
I said nothing that isn't already true. The camera heard it.
Sarge, her record's clear. Normally we'd hand back the card now.
Normally isn't today. The card stays with me until I'm done.
Keep the card. It changes nothing about the seal, Sergeant Hollis.
We'll see. Fifteen minutes is long in a small room.
Let me guess. This started with Ray Pruitt, didn't it?
I'm not going to talk about anyone by name, Sergeant.
Property tech. Quit in August. Hired a lawyer the same week.
People hire lawyers for all kinds of reasons. Mostly ordinary ones.
Not Ray. Ray couldn't afford coffee. Somebody paid for that lawyer.
You've thought about this a great deal, haven't you, Sergeant?
A records request has sat on my desk for three weeks.
Three weeks is long for a records request. Most take days.
Most aren't asking for every property log from twenty-seventeen.
You haven't answered it. That's what three weeks usually means.
I answer when I'm ready. Downstairs runs on my schedule.
It used to. For six weeks, it ran on mine.
Is it Pike Street? Or Delmar? Just tell me which one.
I haven't mentioned a single case. You've mentioned two already.
Calvin Reed. That's the one, isn't it? Somebody's crying about Reed.
Reed was nine years ago. The jury took forty minutes.
I'm not here to argue about any jury. Only about paper.
Paper. You think paper can hurt fourteen years of my work?
Paper doesn't hurt anyone. It remembers what people did to it.
Sarge, maybe we just let her go up. She's expected.
Maybe you just go stand in the hall if you're nervous.
I'm not nervous. I'm only saying she's been patient with us.
Patient people are the ones you watch, Moreno. Remember that one.
Please take your hand off that. It isn't in your custody.
Everything in this room is in my custody. That's my job.
Not this. This was sealed by order of a federal judge.
Then the judge can come down and tell me so himself.
Herself. And she would, but you won't like how it goes.
You think I scare easy? I've been in worse rooms.
I don't want you scared. I want you to hear me.
Go on, then. I'm listening. Moreno's camera is listening too.
If that seal breaks in your hands, it can't go back.
Wax is wax. Anybody can buy a stick of red wax.
The wax isn't the point. The tape and the form are.
Everyone who touches that packet signs the form. Times, names, reasons.
So I sign it too. Sergeant Hollis, opened for review. Simple.
That's exactly what it would say. Forever, on every copy.
Signatures. You people and your signatures. Like ink ever proved anything.
You keep talking like you know what's inside better than me.
I do know. I wrote most of it. That's the difference.
Then there's nothing in there you can't just tell me yourself.
I can't tell you. I'm warning you. Those are different things.
Sounded like a threat. Moreno, did that sound like one?
It sounded like a warning, Sarge. She said it real calm.
Calm. Everybody's calm until the paper's out on the table.
The paper's already on the table. You're the one holding it.
Moreno, get your notebook out. We're writing this up right now.
Subject refused to identify contents of an unlogged item. Write that.
She gave her name, Sarge. And the exhibit number. It's logged.
Not in my ledger, it isn't. So it's unlogged. Write it.
I can write that she asked to log it. That's true.
You've been here six months. You don't decide what happened, son.
The camera decides, Sarge. That's what you told us in training.
I told you a lot. Pick the parts that help you.
Deputy Moreno. You don't have to write anything you didn't see.
Ma'am, with respect, please let me handle my own sergeant.
Fair. Then I'll ask one thing. Please don't stop that camera.
I already told you. It runs the whole shift. That's policy.
Policy. You both love policy until it's your name on something.
I'd like my identification back now, Sergeant. You've checked it.
You'll get it back when that packet's logged properly.
Then write it in properly. Exhibit number, time, my signature, done.
And contents. My ledger has a contents column. Always has.
Your ledger has a column for sealed items too. Page one.
She's right, Sarge. There's a sealed column. I've seen it used.
Moreno, one more word and you're working nights till Christmas.
Yes, Sarge. But the column's still there either way.
Fine. Then the seal comes off, and the column won't matter.
You say that like it's decided. It doesn't have to be.
Who are you working for? Internal affairs? A defense firm?
I work for the court. I've said that three times now.
Courts don't send auditors for nothing. Somebody complained. Who complained?
Nobody complained to me. I counted. Counting doesn't need a complaint.
Counting what? Boxes? I count boxes every Friday. They're all there.
The boxes are all there. That isn't what I was counting.
Then what? Bags? Weights? Signatures? Just tell me what you counted.
Signatures. You were counting my signatures. That's what this is.
Guess all you like. I'm not answering any of it here.
That's not a no. Moreno, you heard. That wasn't a no.
It wasn't a yes. I'm declining a question you can't ask.
I can ask anything I want in my own records room.
You can ask. You can't open. That's where the line is.
Lines. Everybody's got lines for me today. Nobody's got answers.
Here's an answer. It's ten fifty-two. I'm still standing here.
I could have walked out ten minutes ago. I didn't.
Because Moreno would've stopped you. I told him to stop you.
Because walking out breaks the chain. I don't break the chain.
So you need my signature. You need me. Say it.
I need a clean record. Your signature is part of it.
Second time, Sergeant. Opening that won't end what you're afraid of.
It will prove it. With your own hands, on camera.
My camera? That's Moreno's camera. Moreno works for me. Not you.
I hand-carried one of these once. Federal seal. Twenty-eleven, I think.
Then you remember how careful everyone was. Nobody touched the seal.
The captain made me sign three times between car and courtroom.
Three signatures for one envelope. Did you wonder why, back then?
I figured lawyers like paperwork. Lawyers always like their paperwork.
It's not for lawyers. It's for the accused. And the accuser.
A seal means nobody added anything, and nobody took anything away.
And you're telling me nobody's taken anything away from this one.
Not since I signed it at nine. Read the form yourself.
Bell, nine-oh-four. Bell, ten-thirty-eight. That's all it says. Just you.
Just me. So everything inside is exactly as I left it.
Ma'am, can I ask something? What happens if somebody opens it?
Then the next line on that form gets their name.
And the grand jury asks why. The answer goes on record.
Even if they just look? Even if they put it back?
You can't undo it, Deputy. The wax breaks once. Only once.
She wants you scared, Moreno. It's a performance. Don't buy it.
I'm not scared, Sarge. I'm trying to understand what we're doing.
What we're doing is our jobs. Somebody in this room should.
My job ends when that packet reaches 3B, seal whole.
And when does my job end? When your paper says so?
I can't answer that. I only know where mine ends.
Four minutes. You've got four minutes, and so have I, apparently.
Here's what I think. You want me to be afraid.
Afraid men hand things over. I've watched it for years.
I don't want anything handed over. I want you to stop.
Stop what? Asking questions in my own room? Doing my job?
Stop before your hands do something your head hasn't decided yet.
Moreno's watching. The camera's watching. Everyone wants to see me blink.
Nobody wants you to blink. I'd rather you just walked away.
Walk away and wait for a call? I've waited three weeks.
Three weeks of nobody calling. Every morning, waiting for that phone.
I know. That part I'm sorry about. Waiting is hard.
Don't you dare feel sorry for me. Not in my building.
Sarge, please. Let her sign it out. It's not too late.
Too late for what? I need to know what's coming.
This is the third time I'm saying it. Don't open that.
Whatever you think is in there, opening it is worse.
Believe you. A stranger who spent six weeks in my basement.
I won't reach for it again. It's yours now, Sergeant.
Mine. Good. That's the first thing you've said that makes sense.
Moreno, note the time. Ten fifty-eight. Sergeant Hollis reviewing contents.
I'm noting the time, Sarge. And that she warned you.
Note whatever you want. You'll see I was right about her.
Ten fifty-eight. I'll remember that time for a long while.
Ten fifty-eight. Exhibit forty-one, seventeen, A. Seal broken by Sergeant Hollis.
Say it like a newsreader if you want. It's just wax.
Sarge, you actually did it. You actually broke a federal seal.
Sarge? What does it say? You've gone completely white, Sarge.
It's a grand jury cover sheet. Linwood County property room investigation.
The line underneath it names the subject of the investigation.
Whose name, Sarge? Tell me whose name is on that page.
It's a mistake. Somebody typed this wrong. This is all wrong.
Nobody typed it wrong. I checked that line three times.
Six cases. I logged thousands of bags. Thousands of them.
Six where the weights changed before trial. Your signature both times.
Signatures get copied. Anybody could have signed my name on those.
Ray Pruitt watched you sign them. He kept copies nine years.
Ray. Of course it's Ray. He never could keep quiet.
Ray kept quiet nine years. That's the part that broke him.
Ma'am, is that why you needed it sealed? Because of him?
It's sealed because every page has to reach the jury untouched.
Now it reaches them with one new page. His.
I didn't write anything. I opened an envelope. That's all.
On camera. After three warnings. In front of a deputy.
Moreno. Turn that thing off. Just for one minute. Off.
I can't, Sarge. You know I can't. And I won't.
Reed. Calvin Reed is one of the six, isn't he?
He's the first of the six. Nine years in Barlow State.
The bag weighed what it weighed. I wrote what was there.
At intake it was eleven grams. At trial, it was fifty-two.
Eleven grams is a misdemeanor. Fifty-two was nine years. Your handwriting.
You think a number on a form says who I am?
No. But it tells a jury what a man did.
What happens now, ma'am? What am I supposed to do?
That's your call, Deputy. Not mine, and not his. Yours.
Moreno. Eli. Listen to me. Think about your career.
Six months in. Make this call and nobody here trusts you.
Sarge, you taught us the camera decides. It already decided.
I was talking about other people, son. Not about us.
There isn't an us, Sarge. There's just what the camera saw.
Records to 3B. Sealed exhibit opened at the counter. Clerk, please.
They knew she was coming, Sarge. They've been waiting since ten.
Two marshals are coming down. The clerk wants you upstairs.
Upstairs. Fourteen years, and I've never once been called upstairs.
You can walk up yourself, Sergeant. Nobody has to walk you.
Is that a kindness? From you? After everything you've just done?
It's the last choice you still get to make yourself.
Deputy, log it with me. Opened at ten fifty-eight.
Doctor Bell. I didn't think we'd see you down here again.
Just one more signature. The grand jury released the exhibit back.
Two signatures now, for everything. Mine and the clerk's. New rule.
Good rule. Sounds like somebody who learned something. Who wrote it?
The oversight board. I asked them to keep the sealed column.
How are things here? Honestly. Not the version for the board.
Quiet. Some people don't talk to me. Most people do, actually.
And Sergeant Hollis? I heard about the indictment, not much else.
Suspended. His certification's gone. Trial's set for March, they're saying.
He sent me a note. Said I wrote the report right.
That might be the truest thing he's written in years.
Four of the six cases are vacated. Two more by Christmas.
And Mr. Reed? I was told he'd be down here today.
Any minute. He's coming for his property envelope. Nine years shelved.
They told me upstairs to collect my things here. Calvin Reed.
Yes, sir. It's ready. Watch, wallet, keys. Everything's logged.
You're Doctor Bell. My lawyer said you read every page twice.
Three times, Mr. Reed. Some pages I couldn't stop reading.
Nine years I said the weight was wrong. Nobody listened.
It's written down now. In a place nobody gets to change.
I don't know what to say to you. I keep trying.
You don't owe me anything. Sign for your things. They're yours.
